WS2 · Original texts and text complexity

Six Original Texts for Grades 3–5

One topic, three grade levels: animals that change the places they live. Each text was written for this portfolio, and each comes with the analysis I used to place it.

Role
Writer and complexity analyst
Texts
6: three literary, three informational
Grades
3, 4 and 5, two texts each
Settings
Three set in or tied to The Bahamas
Rights
All original; no permissions needed
Label
Representative sample
Look at this first: "The Crunching Sound". Its readability formula says Grade 2. The qualitative analysis explains why it belongs in Grade 4, which is the kind of judgment a formula cannot make.

How I placed each text

I used the three-part model from the Common Core's Appendix A: quantitative measures, qualitative features, and the reader and task. For the quantitative measure I report a Flesch–Kincaid grade estimate, computed with an automated syllable count, and compare it with the grade-band ranges published in the Supplemental Information for Appendix A (2012): about 1.98–5.34 for Grades 2–3 and 4.51–7.73 for Grades 4–5. Formulas only see sentence and word length, so they are a starting point. Where my qualitative judgment differs from the formula, I say why.

Text 1 · Grade 3 · Literary

Big Claw's Burrow

Original text by Barbara Zá Franks · 307 words

1Big Claw was the largest land crab on Pine Lane. Every evening, when the sun slid behind the casuarina trees, she climbed out of her burrow to look for fallen sea grapes.

2Her burrow was her pride. She had dug it herself, one scoop of sand at a time, down and down until the walls felt cool and damp. At the bottom, there was even a little water. On hot days, Big Claw rested there while the rest of Grand Bahama baked in the sun.

3"This burrow is mine," she told everyone who passed. "I dug it. Nobody else comes in."

4One afternoon, the sky turned the color of an old bruise. The wind pushed the palm trees sideways. Rain came down so hard that it bounced.

5Big Claw hurried to her burrow. At the entrance she found a curly-tailed lizard, a little tree frog and a shivering little hermit crab, all pressed against the sand.

6"Please," said the lizard. "The water is rising everywhere. Your burrow is the only deep, safe place on the whole lane."

7Big Claw clicked her claws. She thought about all the work she had done. She thought about how warm and dry it was inside. Then she looked at the hermit crab, whose shell was rocking in the wind.

8"Fine," she grumbled. "But no one touches my sea grapes."

9All night, the storm roared above them. Down in the burrow, it was quiet. The tree frog told stories. The lizard snored. The hermit crab fell asleep against Big Claw's leg, and she found she did not mind at all.

10In the morning, the sun came out and the visitors climbed into the bright, washed world.

11"Thank you," said the hermit crab. "Your burrow saved us."

12Big Claw watched them go. Then she began to dig a little wider, just in case.

QuantitativeFK 2.7, inside the Grades 2–3 range. Short sentences, mostly one- and two-syllable words.
QualitativeMeaning: one clear theme (sharing what you worked for), shown through a character change rather than stated. Structure: chronological, with a classic problem and turn. Language: some figurative language ("the color of an old bruise," "baked in the sun") that is supported by context. Knowledge: local animals and plants (land crab, sea grapes, curly-tailed lizard) that Bahamian readers know and others can picture.
Reader and taskGood for discussing how a character changes (RL.3.3) and for a read-aloud that previews "burrow" and "shelter" before the Grade 4 unit. The last line rewards inference: why does she dig wider?
PlacementGrade 3. Formula and qualitative judgment agree.

Text 2 · Grade 3 · Informational

Tunnels Under the Garden

Original text by Barbara Zá Franks · 255 words

1Dig into a healthy garden and you will probably find an earthworm. It may not look like much. It has no eyes, no legs and no bones. But an earthworm is a hard worker, and it changes the soil in ways that help plants grow.

2Earthworms make tunnels. A worm pushes through the soil by stretching its body forward and then pulling the back end along. As it moves, it leaves a tunnel behind it. Some worms stay near the top of the soil. Others dig deep tunnels that go straight down.

3These tunnels help the soil in two ways. First, they let air in. Plant roots need air, just like we do. Second, the tunnels let rain soak down into the ground instead of running off the top. Water can then reach the roots that need it.

4Earthworms also eat as they dig. They swallow bits of soil and dead leaves. Their bodies break the leaves down. What comes out the other end is called a casting. Castings are full of nutrients, the things plants need to grow strong.

5Earthworms mix the soil, too. They pull leaves to the openings of their tunnels. They bring soil from deep below up to the top. Over time, this mixing spreads nutrients through the soil, a little like stirring a pot of soup.

6So the next time you see an earthworm on the sidewalk after a rain, think about the work it does. Under every garden is a busy world of tunnels, and earthworms are its builders.

QuantitativeFK 2.9, inside the Grades 2–3 range.
QualitativePurpose: explicit, stated in the first paragraph. Structure: a simple explanation with signal words ("First," "Second," "also," "too"). Language: two domain words, "casting" and "nutrients," each defined in the same sentence. Knowledge: familiar topic; one simile ("like stirring a pot of soup") supports the hardest idea.
Reader and taskSuited to RI.3.8 (connections between sentences and paragraphs) and RI.3.3 (cause and effect). Works as the first text in a Grade 3 version of the strand.
PlacementGrade 3. Formula and qualitative judgment agree.

Text 3 · Grade 4 · Informational

One Dam, Many Neighbors

Original text by Barbara Zá Franks · 321 words

1A stream runs through a forest. Its water is shallow and quick. A few fish dart under the rocks, and birds stop to drink at the edge. Then a family of beavers arrives, and over the next few years, almost everything about this place will change.

2Beavers are builders. They cut down small trees with their strong front teeth. They drag the branches into the stream and pack them together with mud and stones. Bit by bit, they build a dam, a wall that blocks the flowing water. The water backs up behind the dam and spreads out into a pond.

3For the beavers, the pond is a fortress. Deep water keeps them safe from predators such as coyotes and bears, which cannot easily follow them underwater. In the middle of the pond, the beavers build a lodge of sticks and mud. Its doors are underwater, so the family can come and go without ever stepping onto land.

4But the beavers are not the only ones who benefit. The slow, still water of the pond warms in the sun. Insects lay their eggs in it, and fish and frogs come to eat the insects. Ducks and herons arrive to eat the fish and frogs. Around the edges, the ground stays soggy, and new plants take root. The quick little stream has become a wetland, one of the busiest kinds of habitat on Earth.

5Scientists have a name for animals that change a habitat so much that other living things depend on the change. They call them ecosystem engineers. The beaver is one of the best-known examples. One dam can turn a quiet stream into a home for many kinds of plants and animals, from tiny water beetles to moose.

6The next time you see a pond in the woods, look closely at its edge. You might find a wall of sticks and mud, and the work of a family of engineers.

QuantitativeFK 4.7, at the low end of the Grades 4–5 range.
QualitativePurpose: explicit, but the central concept (ecosystem engineer) is held back until paragraph 5, so readers must connect the earlier examples to the term. Structure: cause and effect, chained across paragraphs (dam, pond, warm water, insects, fish, birds, plants). Language: domain words "predators," "lodge," "wetland," "habitat," "ecosystem engineers," mostly defined in context; one metaphor ("the pond is a fortress"). Knowledge: assumes readers know what a stream and a forest are; no prior science needed.
Reader and taskThe cause-and-effect chain makes it the right anchor for RI.4.3 (explain what happened and why). Placed first in the unit so every later text can be compared with it.
PlacementGrade 4. The formula is at the low end, but the delayed concept and the multi-step causal chain raise the qualitative demand.

Text 4 · Grade 4 · Literary

The Crunching Sound

Original text by Barbara Zá Franks · 287 words

1Kiara floated face down in the clear water off Taino Beach, breathing through her snorkel. Below her, the reef spread out like a garden: purple sea fans, brain coral as round as a pumpkin, and fish everywhere.

2Then she heard it. Crunch. Crunch. Crunch.

3She lifted her head. "Uncle Desmond! Something down there is breaking the coral!"

4Her uncle swam over and pushed his mask up. He had been diving on this reef since he was younger than Kiara. "Show me."

5Kiara pointed. A fish as long as her arm, bright blue with flashes of pink, was pressed against a rock. Each time it opened its mouth, there was that sound again. Crunch.

6"It's wrecking the reef," Kiara said. "Can't we stop it?"

7Uncle Desmond smiled around his snorkel. "Watch a little longer."

8The fish moved along the rock, biting and scraping. Then a small white cloud drifted out behind it and sank slowly to the bottom.

9Kiara wrinkled her nose. "Did it just..."

10"It did," her uncle laughed. "That's a parrotfish. It scrapes off the green stuff, the algae, and it swallows bits of rock too. Then it grinds the rock up and, well, you saw. That white cloud is sand."

11Kiara stared at the white sand on the bottom. She thought of the beach behind her, long and pale and soft.

12"So the beach..." she began.

13"Some of it, yes. And by eating the algae, the parrotfish keeps it from smothering the coral. That crunching is one of the sounds of a healthy reef."

14Kiara put her face back in the water. The parrotfish was still working, crunch after crunch. This time she did not want to stop it. She wanted to say thank you.

QuantitativeFK 1.8, below the Grades 4–5 range. Dialogue makes sentences very short, which pulls the formula down.
QualitativeMeaning: the key event is never stated. Readers must infer what the "small white cloud" is from Kiara's reaction and her uncle's laugh, then follow her change from wanting to stop the fish to wanting to thank it. Structure: a single scene with a misunderstanding and a reversal. Language: sensory and figurative ("spread out like a garden," onomatopoeia); an unfinished sentence ("So the beach...") that asks the reader to complete the thought. Knowledge: embeds the same science as the informational text "The Sand Makers" (WS1), so the pair supports comparing how literary and informational texts present one topic.
Reader and taskRL.4.3 (describe a character using specific details) and RI.4.9-style comparison with the paired informational text.
PlacementGrade 4, above the formula. The inference load, implied humor and the paired-text task make it a Grade 4 text despite short sentences. This is exactly where a single readability score would misplace a text.

Text 5 · Grade 5 · Informational

When Engineers Cause Trouble

Original text by Barbara Zá Franks · 293 words

1Ecosystem engineers are often described as heroes. Beavers create wetlands, gopher tortoises shelter hundreds of species, and parrotfish help keep coral reefs healthy. But an engineer's effects depend on where it is working. In the wrong place, the same building skills can cause serious harm.

2Consider Tierra del Fuego, a group of islands at the southern tip of South America. In the 1940s, a small number of North American beavers were brought there in the hope of starting a fur trade. The fur business never succeeded, but the beavers did. With few predators to hunt them, their numbers grew, and they spread from island to island. Today tens of thousands of beavers live there.

3The forests of Tierra del Fuego did not evolve with beavers. In North America, many trees along streams can sprout again after a beaver cuts them down. Many of the trees in Tierra del Fuego cannot recover the same way. Where beavers have built dams, whole stretches of forest have flooded and died, leaving gray, standing trunks. Scientists who study the region describe it as one of the largest changes to these forests in thousands of years.

4Argentina and Chile, the two countries that share Tierra del Fuego, have worked together on plans to remove the beavers and restore the damaged land. It is a difficult and costly job. It shows that an animal's effect on an environment is not simply good or bad. It depends on the animal, the place, and the other living things that share it.

5The same beaver that builds a home for hundreds of species in one place can tear a forest apart in another. When scientists ask whether an ecosystem engineer is helpful or harmful, the honest answer usually begins with: "It depends."

QuantitativeFK 7.4, at the high end of the Grades 4–5 range.
QualitativePurpose: complicates the unit's earlier message; readers must hold two ideas at once (engineers help; engineers harm). Structure: claim, extended example, explanation of cause, conclusion that returns to the claim. Language: academic phrasing ("did not evolve with," "restore," "costly"), a place name, and a concluding quotation that summarizes the argument. Knowledge: depends on knowing how beavers change land from Text 3; without it, the text is much harder.
Reader and taskRI.5.8 (how an author uses reasons and evidence) and RI.5.9 (integrate several texts). In Grade 4, it is read last, with support, after students know beavers well.
PlacementGrade 5, and a Grade 4 stretch text at the end of the unit. Knowledge built by Texts 3 and WS1's other texts is what makes it reachable.

Text 6 · Grade 5 · Literary

Rebuilding the Reef

Original text by Barbara Zá Franks · 299 words

1The coral nursery looked nothing like Malik had imagined. He had pictured a garden. Instead, rows of white plastic frames, shaped like small trees, stood on the sandy bottom twenty feet below the boat, and from every branch hung a fragment of coral no bigger than his thumb.

2"Every one of those started as a broken piece," said Ms. Ferguson, the volunteer coordinator, as she checked his dive gear for the second time. "Storms snap them off. Boats break them. We collect the pieces that are still alive, hang them here where the water moves and the parrotfish can't nibble them, and wait."

3"How long?" Malik asked.

4"Months. Sometimes a year." She handed him a mesh bag. "Patience is most of the job."

5That morning, Malik's task was simple and, he soon discovered, maddening. He floated beside one frame with a soft brush and cleaned the algae that crept over the plastic, careful not to touch the living coral. The current kept nudging him off position. Twice he drifted into the next row and had to kick back, his breath loud in his ears. By the time Ms. Ferguson signaled to surface, he had cleaned only half a tree.

6On the boat, he pulled off his mask, discouraged. "That's it? A whole dive for half a frame?"

7Ms. Ferguson pointed to a clipboard covered in dates and numbers. "That frame went in last spring. Look." She showed him a photograph: a bare stub of coral the size of a fingernail. Then she pointed over the side, toward the tree he had been cleaning, where the same coral, now a branching fist of tan and gold, swayed in the current.

8Malik leaned over the rail for a long moment.

9"Next week," he said, "I want to try the whole frame."

QuantitativeFK 3.5, below the Grades 4–5 range.
QualitativeMeaning: theme of patience shown, not told; Malik's final line signals a change the reader must interpret. Structure: a time shift carried by a photograph (last spring versus now) that readers must track. Language: longer, layered sentences in narration ("and, he soon discovered, maddening"), precise verbs, and some technical vocabulary (nursery, fragment, current). Knowledge: coral restoration may be unfamiliar; enough is explained in dialogue to follow it.
Reader and taskRL.5.2 (theme from how a character responds to a challenge) and RL.5.3 (compare characters). Also the source for the community adaptation in WS11.
PlacementGrade 5, above the formula, because of the time shift, the implied theme and the layered narration.
